Anchor.Text: one folder per component under public/components

Applied.Outcome: AngularJS components, one folder each with script, template and stylesheet; State and events as the interface; the CLAUDE.md naming exception is in.

Replies.Text:
What a component is, in code. Today the page is one index.html of about 900 lines, with a controller per section (SidebarController, TabsController, HeaderController, ReadController, EditController, ThreadsController and so on) sharing the State factory and talking through $rootScope broadcasts. AngularJS 1.8 has .component() for exactly this: a name, a template, a controller with bindings, and it is already in the page.

I recommend: one folder per component under public/components/<name>/, holding <name>.js (the .component registration and its controller), <name>.html (the template, loaded by templateUrl; no build step, one fetch each, cached) and <name>.css (its styles, one link tag each; consensus.css keeps only the page, the palette and the shared classes). index.html becomes a skeleton of component tags. Every component takes what it shows through bindings or the State service and reports through events, and its header comment names both: that is its interface.

One snag with the house style: Angular registers a component under a camelCase name and matches it as a kebab-case tag (.component( 'threadCard' ) is <thread-card>); a PascalCase name would not match a usable tag. I recommend an exception written into CLAUDE.md: the registration name is Angular's camelCase, the tag is kebab-case, and nothing else is camelCase. The alternative is single-word lowercase names only (tree, tabs, header, threads), which gets awkward at thread-transcript.
all good. give me the change needed for CLAUDE.md and I will make it.

The change for CLAUDE.md, two pieces. Under Naming Conventions, after the camelCase line:

```
- The one exception is AngularJS registration: Angular derives a tag from the name it is registered under, so a component is registered under Angular's camelCase name (`.component( 'threadCard', ... )`) and used as the kebab-case tag (`<thread-card>`), and a binding's name maps to its attribute the same way (`thread` to `thread="..."`). Keep binding names to one word where you can. The registration name and the binding names are the only camelCase in the code; the controller, its functions and its variables follow the rules above.
```

Under Platform Preferences, Web, after the AngularJS + Bootstrap line:

```
- Build the front end as AngularJS components: one folder per component under `public/components/<name>/`, holding `<name>.js` (the registration and its controller), `<name>.html` (the template, loaded by templateUrl) and `<name>.css` (its styles). A component takes what it shows through bindings or the State service, reports through events, and its header comment names both.
```

Anchor.Text: the desktop window uses Electron's hidden title bar with the native overlay buttons

Applied.Outcome: Electron's hidden title bar with the native overlay buttons in the desktop; the same bar without buttons in a browser.

Replies.Text:
The desktop uses Electron's native frame: the OS title bar and buttons, and a native menu bar (Server, View, Quit). A browser has no chrome of ours at all. Window Size/Close buttons of our own mean a frameless window.

I recommend Electron's middle way: titleBarStyle "hidden" with titleBarOverlay, which keeps the native minimize, maximize and close buttons (drawn by Electron, coloured from our palette, and they follow the theme) and gives the rest of the bar to the page as a drag region. Our Title Bar component fills that region; in a browser the same component shows without the window buttons and without the drag region. Fully custom buttons over IPC are more code for the same result, and on a Mac the traffic lights should stay native anyway.

Is the chrome meant for the desktop only, with the browser showing the Title Bar as an ordinary top bar? I assume yes.

Anchor.Text: Each step extracts components and changes no behaviour

Applied.Outcome: Six steps, each a commit with a design thread first; the server tests untouched, the smoke at every step.

Replies.Text:
The shape of the build. The point is to end with the same app, componentized, so each step extracts components and changes no behaviour, except where a thread above decides one (the global filter, the app menu, the chrome). I recommend this order, each step a commit, with a design thread on its line first as before:

1. The scaffold: the components folder, the loading of templates and styles, the CLAUDE.md note on names, and the first extraction, Item Thread Filters and Item Threads (items 6 and 7), the most self-contained part.
2. The Documents Pane: the Tab Bar, the Editor Header with its location line, the html-view used by Read and by the preview, the Monaco editor, the Revisions view, the LLM and Waiting views as tab contents (items 4, 5.1 to 5.3).
3. The CodeMirror editor with its anchors and the setting (item 5.4).
4. The Project Tree and its parts (item 3).
5. The Application Title and the Application Chrome, with the desktop's menu and title bar changes (items 1 and 2).
6. The guide and its pictures, the help, the smokes.

Tests: the 180 node tests are the server's and keep passing untouched; the page has the Electron smokes over DevTools only. I recommend each step ends with that smoke and a look at the page, as the UI Tweaks plans did, and no test framework added for the components.
